books.section: Topic 4.2 The Rise of Political Parties and the Era of Jefferson, C. The Louisiana Purchase and Territorial Expansion

stimulus.source_note: The Louisiana Purchase treaty, 1803, in its embroidered presentation binding bearing the seal of the United States. U.S. National Archives, via Wikimedia Commons. Public domain.
stimulus.text: The Louisiana Purchase treaty, signed in Paris in 1803, shown in its embroidered presentation binding bearing the seal of the United States. By the treaty France sold the Louisiana Territory to the United States for $15 million.

source: original; stimulus image from the shared pool, the Louisiana Purchase treaty binding (1803), public domain
stem: The treaty shown in the image most directly resulted in which of the following?

options.text: The United States gained Florida from Spain
options.misconception: Florida came later, by the Adams-Onis Treaty of 1819, not by the Louisiana Purchase.

options.text: The boundary with Canada was settled at the 49th parallel
options.misconception: The Oregon boundary was settled in 1846, more than forty years after this treaty.

options.text: The territory of the United States roughly doubled in size

options.misconception: French claims in Canada had ended with the Seven Years' War in 1763, not with this treaty.

rationales.A: Florida came later, by the Adams-Onis Treaty of 1819, not by the Louisiana Purchase.
rationales.B: The Oregon boundary was settled in 1846, more than forty years after this treaty.
rationales.C: The purchase added about 828,000 square miles west of the Mississippi, roughly doubling the nation's size for $15 million. Background: the price worked out to about three cents an acre, and the new land included the fertile Great Plains and full control of New Orleans.
rationales.D: French claims in Canada had ended with the Seven Years' War in 1763, not with this treaty.
rationales.general:
1. Read the image. A treaty of 1803, by which France sold Louisiana.
2. Ask how big Louisiana was. About 828,000 square miles west of the Mississippi.
3. Compare it to the old United States. The purchase roughly doubled the nation's size.
4. Put it together. One treaty, signed in Paris, made the country twice as large.
Remember: when a treaty moves land, ask how much land and what it cost.
